sources.title: The Thames Tunnel: Marc Brunel's engineering marvel (London Museum)

youtube.title: Thames Tunnel: How a Worm Helped Dig Under a River
youtube.description:
The Thames Tunnel was the first tunnel ever successfully built under a navigable river, and it almost killed the man who later became Britain's most famous engineer. How did a father and son beat the River Thames with an idea copied from a worm?

In 1825 Marc Brunel started digging from Rotherhithe to Wapping with his new tunnelling shield: an iron frame with 36 cells, one miner in each. The river broke in again and again, young Isambard Kingdom Brunel nearly drowned in the 1828 flood, and the half-finished tunnel sat bricked up for seven years. It finally opened in 1843, and trains still run through it today on the London Overground.

In this video:
- Why nobody could build a bridge or a tunnel there
- The shipworm that inspired the tunnelling shield
- The banquet under the river and the flood of 1828
- Seven years of silence and the opening day crowds

Subscribe to Stickstory for more true stories about how things were built. Would you have paid a penny to walk under the Thames in 1843? Tell me in the comments!

#thamestunnel #brunel #londonhistory #engineering #stickstory

scenes.text: January 1828. Deep under the River Thames, a young engineer heard a sound no tunnel should ever make.
scenes.visual: Cut-away of the Thames at night-dim: ships drift on the surface, warehouses on both banks, and deep below the riverbed the lit brick tunnel reaches halfway across; on 'sound' the mud above the shield shakes and the first water starts to trickle down; red note '1828'.

scenes.text: The river was coming in. Water roared out of the dark, faster than anyone could run, and the lamps went out one by one.
scenes.visual: Same tunnel: on 'coming' a wall of water rolls from the far end toward us, the lamps die from far to near on 'lamps'; the fez narrator in the foreground jumps back in shock on 'roared'.

scenes.text: He was only twenty-one. His name was Isambard Kingdom Brunel, and he was about to drown under London.
scenes.visual: Close on the young engineer at the shield deep in the tunnel, water rising around him; hand note 'Isambard K. Brunel, 21' with an arrow on 'Isambard'.

scenes.text: So why would anyone dig under a river with tools from the 1820s? And how on earth did they ever finish it?
scenes.visual: Giant words 'Why dig' / 'under a river?' set word by word with 'river' in a red box; the fez narrator on the right points at them, then shrugs.

scenes.text: To understand that, you have to see the Thames back then.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 1 / 5 card: blue disc with 1, title 'A River Full of Ships' with a hand-drawn underline.

scenes.text: It was one of the busiest rivers on the planet, packed with sailing ships from bank to bank.
scenes.visual: Cut-away of the Thames between Rotherhithe and Wapping: warehouses on both banks, five sailing ships drift across the surface, riverbed mud below with no tunnel yet; red note 'busiest river' on 'busiest'.

scenes.text: A bridge down here? Forget it. The tall masts had to get through.
scenes.visual: On the busy quay the fez narrator holds up a sign 'NO BRIDGE', then points up at the tall masts of a big sailing ship passing behind him on 'masts'.

scenes.text: So if you wanted to cross with a cart, you went the long way round, to London Bridge.
scenes.visual: Old map of the Thames bend: north bank and south bank, Rotherhithe and Wapping facing each other across the water; a red dashed cart route runs from Rotherhithe all the way west to London Bridge and back east to Wapping; note 'the long way round'.

scenes.text: People had tried to go under the river before. Around 1807, Cornish miners, Richard Trevithick among them, dug a narrow test passage.
scenes.visual: River cut-away: a narrow timber-propped test passage creeps from the left shaft under the riverbed; note 'Trevithick, 1807' on 'Trevithick'.

scenes.text: They got most of the way across. Then the river broke in, twice, and the project died.
scenes.visual: Same cut-away: the passage is nearly across when on 'broke' the riverbed opens and water pours down and floods it back to the shaft; red stamp 'FLOODED x2' on 'twice'.

scenes.text: The verdict was brutal: a tunnel under the Thames was impossible.
scenes.visual: Giant words 'A tunnel here?' / 'Impossible.' with 'Impossible.' in a red box; hand note 'the experts, 1809'.

scenes.text: But one man refused to believe it, and he found his answer inside a piece of rotten wood.
scenes.visual: Close cut through an old ship timber riddled with shell-lined holes; the fez narrator in front looks at it through binoculars, then points at it on 'wood'.

scenes.text: His name was Marc Brunel, Isambard's father, a French engineer living in London.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 2 / 5 card: blue disc with 2, title 'A Worm's Idea' with a hand-drawn underline.

scenes.text: He had been looking at ship timber eaten through by the shipworm.
scenes.visual: Timber cut: a shipworm with a long soft body bores its way forward from the left, leaving a shell-lined tunnel; note 'shipworm' with an arrow on 'shipworm'.

scenes.text: It bores into wood with two hard shell plates on its head, and as it moves forward, it lines the hole behind it.
scenes.visual: Close-up on the worm's head: two blue shell plates rock and grind the wood, sawdust flies; on 'lines' the white shell lining of the tunnel behind it gets a note 'lining'.

scenes.text: And Brunel thought: what if men could do the same? In 1818 he patented the tunnelling shield.
scenes.visual: In a candle-lit study, Marc Brunel (grey beard) points at a drawing board; the fez narrator beside him holds up a sign 'PATENT 1818' on '1818'.

scenes.text: Picture a giant iron frame, as tall as a house, pressed against the mud. It had thirty-six cells, one miner in each.
scenes.visual: The shield seen from the tunnel draws itself column by column: a huge iron frame of three storeys pressed against the wet mud, lamps above, drips falling; on 'thirty' miners pop into the 36 cells one by one while a big red counter ticks up to '36 cells'.

scenes.text: A miner pulled out one small board, dug away a few inches of clay, and put the board back.
scenes.visual: Close-up on one cell: on 'pulled' a red ring circles it, the middle board slides out, the miner digs at the clay behind it, and on 'back' the board slides back in.

scenes.text: Then screws pushed the whole frame forward, and bricklayers closed the ring right behind it, so the mud never stood naked for long.
scenes.visual: Cut-away close on the head of the tunnel: red arrows push the shield forward on 'screws', and new brick rings flash in right behind it on 'bricklayers'.

scenes.text: In 1825 the digging began at Rotherhithe, and on a good week they moved a few feet. Slow, but it worked. Or so they thought.
scenes.visual: Wide cut-away: from the Rotherhithe shaft the brick tunnel crawls a short way under the river as ships pass above; note '1825' on 'digging' and red note '1 to 8 feet a week' on 'week'.

scenes.text: Because now the river started fighting back.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 3 / 5 card: blue disc with 3, title 'The River Fights Back' with a hand-drawn underline.

scenes.text: The water seeping in was basically London's sewage. Men fell sick, and gas from the mud could catch fire on the miners' lamps.
scenes.visual: Inside the half-built tunnel, dirty water drips from the arches onto the miners at the shield; on 'fire' a wall lamp bursts into a red and gold gas flame.

scenes.text: Even Marc Brunel fell ill, so his son Isambard, only twenty, ran the whole dig.
scenes.visual: A bedroom by the works: old Marc Brunel sits sick in bed under a blue blanket, looking worried; his young son Isambard walks in carrying the plans, then points ahead; note 'Isambard, 20'.

scenes.text: Meanwhile, curious Londoners paid a shilling just to come down and watch the shield.
scenes.visual: Visitors in top hats and long dresses stroll down the lit tunnel toward the working shield; red note '1 shilling' on 'shilling'.

scenes.text: In May 1827, the river broke through for the first time.
scenes.visual: River cut-away: the brick tunnel is under the middle of the river when on 'broke' the riverbed above the shield opens and water pours down into it; red note 'May 1827'.

scenes.text: Isambard went down in a diving bell to find the hole, and they plugged it with bags of clay.
scenes.visual: From a boat above the breach a diving bell is lowered on a rope to the riverbed, then clay bags drop one by one into the hole on 'bags'.

scenes.text: Then, to prove the tunnel was safe, the company threw a banquet inside it. Long tables and candlelight, under the Thames!
scenes.visual: Inside the tunnel a long banquet table with a red cloth sets itself down the middle, candles lit, guests seated both sides; the fez narrator in the foreground throws up his arms in delight on 'banquet'; note 'under the river!' on 'under'.

scenes.text: Two months later, the river came back, much harder.
scenes.visual: Over a stormy river: giant words 'The river' / 'came back' with 'back' in a red box; red note 'January 1828'.

scenes.text: Isambard was at the shield with two miners when the ground above them gave way. The water hit like a wall.
scenes.visual: Close on the far shield: Isambard and two miners dig at the face; on 'gave' a wall of water bursts from the shield and rolls down the tunnel at us while a miner runs toward us with his lantern; the lamps die.

scenes.text: A falling timber trapped his leg, the water nearly swept him away, and he was pulled out unconscious.
scenes.visual: Close: a heavy timber falls across the flooded tunnel on 'timber', the water rises around Isambard, and on 'pulled' another worker grabs him and drags him clear.

scenes.text: Six men died that day, including the two who had been beside him.
scenes.visual: Quiet card: giant words 'Six men' / 'never came home' with 'Six' in a red box, over a dark river.

scenes.text: Isambard was badly hurt, and he never worked on the tunnel again. And then came the worst part. Nothing happened at all.
scenes.visual: Night by the tunnel shaft: Isambard limps away on a crutch, head down; the fez narrator steps in, thinks, then shrugs on 'Nothing'.

scenes.text: In August 1828, they bricked up the tunnel face and walked away.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 4 / 5 card: blue disc with 4, title 'Seven Years of Silence' with a hand-drawn underline.

scenes.text: Half a tunnel sat under the river, in the dark, for seven years.
scenes.visual: River cut-away at night-dim: the tunnel ends halfway under the river at a red brick wall that builds itself on 'half'; its lamps are out; ships keep drifting above; red note '1828 to 1835' on 'seven'.

scenes.text: Marc Brunel kept knocking on doors, and finally the government lent the money.
scenes.visual: A London street: old Marc Brunel knocks on a big door, again and again; on 'government' a hand note 'Treasury loan, 1834' appears and the fez narrator holds up a sign 'LOAN!' on 'money'.

scenes.text: Here's the thing, though: the old shield was worn out. So Brunel built a new, heavier one, and the miners went back into the mud.
scenes.visual: A new, heavier riveted shield draws itself column by column; on 'miners' the cells fill with miners again; note 'new shield, 1836'.

scenes.text: And the river broke in again. Four more times! But this time they were ready, and they kept going.
scenes.visual: Cut-away: water bursts down through the riverbed into the tunnel on 'broke'; red stamp 'x4' on 'Four'; then the shield pushes on, new rings flashing, on 'going'.

scenes.text: In November 1841, the shield finally reached Wapping, on the other side. Was it worth it?
scenes.visual: Cut-away: the brick tunnel crawls the last stretch and meets the Wapping shaft on the far bank on 'Wapping'; red note 'Nov 1841'.

scenes.text: On the 25th of March, 1843, the Thames Tunnel opened, and London went crazy.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 5 / 5 card: blue disc with 5, title 'The Eighth Wonder' with a hand-drawn underline.

scenes.text: About fifty thousand people walked through on the very first day.
scenes.visual: The finished tunnel, lamps lit and stalls along the walls: a stream of visitors walks away from us down the arches; big red '50,000' on 'fifty'.

scenes.text: A million came in the first ten weeks, roughly half of London, at a penny each.
scenes.visual: At the tunnel entrance a toll booth with a '1 PENNY' sign; a gold penny drops on the counter on 'penny'; visitors stream down the tunnel; red stamp '1,000,000' on 'million' and note 'half of London' on 'half'.

scenes.text: People called it the eighth wonder of the world.
scenes.visual: Giant words 'The eighth' / 'wonder' with 'eighth' in a red box; the fez narrator on the right points at it, delighted.

scenes.text: There was just one problem. It was built for horses and carts, but the money ran out before the ramps.
scenes.visual: The engineer's drawing board on his desk: a cut-away of the tunnel with a spiral cart ramp winding down each shaft, both labelled 'cart ramp'; Marc Brunel points at them; on 'ramps' both ramps get a big red cross; note 'no money' on 'money'.

scenes.text: So for over twenty years, it was a tunnel for walking, with stalls and fairs inside.
scenes.visual: Inside the tunnel striped market stalls line both walls, people stroll in both directions; note 'stalls and fairs'.

scenes.text: Then, in 1869, the trains came. And here's the best part: they never left. Today, London Overground trains still run through Brunel's tunnel.
scenes.visual: Rails appear in the tunnel; on '1869' a steam engine rolls out of the dark towards us, smoke puffing; red note '1869' and on 'Today' the note 'still running today'.

scenes.text: And every giant tunnel boring machine under our cities still works the same way: a shield at the front, a lining right behind. An idea borrowed from a worm.
scenes.visual: Back in the timber: the shipworm bores on, and on 'shield' a red shield grid lays itself over its head; note 'same idea' on 'worm'.

scenes.text: So, would you have paid a penny to walk under the Thames in 1843? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe to Stickstory for more true stories like this.
scenes.visual: The lit tunnel full of strolling visitors and stalls; the fez narrator in the foreground holds up a big penny coin on 'penny', then waves goodbye on 'subscribe'.
